utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I have one brief preliminary matter. There was a list of exhibits the Prosecution would like to introduce in the context of the cross-examination of Witness Milosevic. That list has now been verified, and I do think that on that list there are 13 documents or 13 items which are sought to be MFI'd for the time being. Madam Registrar, would you please so kind to make a list of those 13 provisionally assigned numbers so that the Defence can express itself on admission.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Then I'd like to briefly turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Petrovic, your next witness will be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Our next witness is Rade Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, I take it. Mr. Vujovic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Vujovic, before you'll be examined by the parties, I have to raise a matter about protective measures. We've heard from counsel for Mr. Simatovic that you personally do not seek any protective measures. On the 8th of May of this year, the Republic of Serbia has requested protective measures; most important, they were seeking closed session, and that your identity be protected at all times. Now, in line with the common practice of this Chamber, we have denied Serbia's request for the protective measures as sought, but, at the same time, we would like to instruct you, and I similarly instruct the parties, that you should ask for private session - therefore, the evidence not to be heard in public - if the question or if your answers would reveal the identity of, one, a BIA source; or if it would reveal the identity of a BIA operative; or, third category, a location used by the BIA. So if that would be part of your answer, we would invite you to go in private session. In addition to these three category, if specific technical means used by the BIA would be touched upon in your answer or in the questions, and that is, technical means, specific technical means used for intelligence-gathering purposes, then we would also like you to ask for private session so that this information, BIA, source, BIA operative, BIA location or specific technical means would be discussed. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to inform the Republic of Serbia of the decision by the Chamber. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I give you an opportunity to start, I do understand that the witness has asked for a piece of paper and a pen so that he can make notes when being examined. I take it that there's no problem with that, Ms. Friedman, Mr. Jordash. So, therefore, could someone provide the witness with a pen and paper. Mr. Vujovic, you will first be examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. And if at any time you would need a break or any rest, don't hesitate to address me. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vujovic. Could you please tell us your name for the record as well as the date and place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Rade Vujovic. I was born on 3rd of March, 1952, in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you went to the elementary school and secondary school?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the elementary school in Pec and then I graduated from the grammar school in Belgrade, and also from the university in Belgrade with a degree in technical sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that you graduated with a degree in electrical engineering. What was your speciality?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: It was electronics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the army, in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in 1978 and 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was your first job?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: After I graduated, I taught at the secondary school, Rade Koncar, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you joined the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1980. I started working at the Federal Secretariat of Internal Affairs at the State Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was your position in the state security? When you first joined, what was your first position?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I started working as a junior engineer. That was the entry position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which organisational unit did you join when you started working at the state security?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: That was the administration for the application of operative technique with -- in the State Security Department of the Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After that, after having been a junior engineer, how did your career evolve? What other positions did you occupy?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: First, I was a junior engineer, then I was an associates engineer, an independent engineer, the chief engineer, and then when I joined the federal service I was the chief of the first department in the 7th Administration, which was the administration for the application of operative techniques.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you became an employee of the State Security Department of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in 1992 when there was a merger between the federal MUP and the republican MUP. Then I joined the MUP of Serbia, its security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you joined, what was your position in the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: The same position. I remained the chief of the first department in the 7th Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were promoted within the State Security Department in the Republic of Serbia? Were you assigned other duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I was there from 1992 until 1994 as the chief of department. And then I was appointed the chief of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left your position in the State Security Department of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, something happened. There was a shake-up. The then-chief of the security department, Mr. Stanisic, was removed, and I was also removed from my position as the chief of administration, and I was appointed the chief of section in the state security. I did not accept that position and I simply resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, the record is not really clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That new post which you were assigned, where was that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: That was part of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you remain in that position to which you were assigned in the public security?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No. I resigned. And I left the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you do then? When you left the MUP of Serbia, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: For the next three years, I worked for a company that represented Motorola in Serbia. It was a privately owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you joined the MUP of Serbia again, i.e., when you rejoined the state security sector?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In 2001, the newly appointed chief, Andrija Savic, invited me to an interview and he asked me whether I would be interested in joining the new management team of the State Security Department. He wanted me to be a member of that team. I agreed. And then he informed me that Prime Minister Djindjic gave his consent, and then I rejoined the department as the deputy chief for operative equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did you work for the State Security Department?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I remained there until 2005. And in the meantime I was appointed the chief of security institute, and then in 2005, I was pensioned off at my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the State Security Department was transformed and became a different agency?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: The department was part of the Ministry of Internal Affairs until 2002, and then it was reorganised, and the State Security Department left, as it were, the MUP, and it became a special agency. And from then, its name was security and information or intelligence agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session, I'm not sure if there's a reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Registry is of the opinion that we're not in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm misinformed then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujovic. After having dealt with your CV, I would like to put a few specific questions to you in relation to your work while you were still employed there. While you worked in the federal ministry dealing with operative equipment, as far as the application of this equipment is concerned, what was it that was actually done by the federal security service?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, this kind of work with operative equipment falls into two groups: One is the offensive group, if you will, and the other one is the defensive work -- group. Offensive is the work that is done in order to collect information and then document that, TV, video, et cetera, so that is one group of this kind of work. Another group that is also very important, and a lot of people work on that, too, has to do with defensive work, if you will: Anti-sabotage, sanitary, chemistry biological protection, electronic protection of buildings, mechanical protection, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The federal State Security Service what kind of relationship did it have with the security services in the republics and provinces in terms of functionality? Was it based on subordination? Was it a different kind of relationship? Could you please tell us what it was like.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that it was a classical relationship of subordination. It was co-ordination and guidance; primarily co-operation, accommodation of views, and so on. However, the federal service worked independently within its own purview, and I'm talking about the field of operative equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the work that was done independently at federal level?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as operative equipment was concerned, it was the application of all measures, offensive and defensive. All of that was done independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as operative measures are concerned that were applied by the federal service, which structures were the subject of interest of the federal service, as far as operative measures were concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In the organisation of the state security, in the SFRY, while that state was still in existence, the federal service was primarily oriented towards diplomacy. So, as far as offensive measures were concerned, that had to do with the diplomatic, and it was basically focussed on the territory of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1991, can you tell us how senior personnel were recruited in the federal service? Up until 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: All the republics and provinces had to be represented properly in senior posts, so basically all the senior personnel came from the different republics and provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us until when the senior personnel who came from republics that had opted out of Yugoslavia remained in their positions in the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1992. One day, basically they all left Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the situation was in the federal service after senior personnel from the cessationists republics left?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, objectively speaking, we were in a state of vacuum, a state that had not been fully defined. We were simply waiting to see what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In that period, after they had left, could you tell us what these senior posts were, that were vacated by the people who left? Were these significant positions or --

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: People from the republics were appointed to the most senior positions. Zdravko Mustac, a Croat, headed the service itself and then the head of the important department, the first one, was a Slovene and then the head of the analytical department also hailed from a different republic. So the people who were from Serbia stayed on, but the others who, in my view, held the key positions in state security hailed from different republics, those that had left the SFRY and these persons left too. They returned to their republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that the key senior personnel left, and you referred to this vacuum that remained in the service. How did this reflect on the everyday functioning of the service, defining tasks, managing work as such?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we continued on the basis of inertia. We stayed in the buildings where we were, but all of us who stayed on in the federal MUP realised that the role of the federal service had to be redefined. The situation was a completely new one. This state was no longer in existence. And what had to be defined was what this new federal service was supposed to be; if it were to stay on in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established in April 1992, were security services brought together at the level of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No. This period of vacuum continued. We all discussed this, and we received some information to the effect that the key question was the decision of Montenegro as a federal unit, in terms of whether they wanted to take part in the restructuring the State Security Service or not, and it went back and forth: They wanted to; they didn't want to. And these discussions took place basically on a daily basis. It went on for a very long time. Too long, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This period that you've been talking about, the period of vacuum, as you call it, in very practical terms, how many services were there in the territory of the Republic of Serbia that were doing the same kind of work or almost the same?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: That was a paradox. In the territory of Serbia, you had two State Security Services that were doing the same kind of work or similar work. In addition to that, you also had a service that independently took measures in the territory of Serbia. So for who?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In this period of time, the federal State Security Service, in this period of vacuum that you referred to, did it have any kind of powers in the territory of the Republic of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No. We could not act independently in the territory of the Republic of Montenegro. I'm referring to operative equipment. In the territory of Belgrade, we acted independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it normal, customary, is that the usual thing for there to be two parallel services in the territory of one and the same country dealing with the same kind of work or similar work?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, no such thing existed anywhere. And that is absurd. It's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, at one point in time, did the federal service and the service of the Republic of Serbia merge?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In the Autumn of 1992, these two services merged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that looked like in your very own case, from the point of view of your very own job?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you leave your office? Was your documentation taken over? Were you expelled? Did you lose your job? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: None of the above. In my specific case and in my department, as well, in the morning we had collegium meetings. I came to work. We had a collegium meeting of our department. Our superior told us that the decision had been made concerning this merge, and that we should see how people should work and how jobs should be distributed and what kind of work should be given to the people would come from the republic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone take over your work documentation? Were you banned from any of the premises that you used for your daily work?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No. That did not happen to me, and it didn't really happen to anyone within the 7th Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, was anybody expelled from the State Security Service? Did they lose their jobs? Were they dismissed?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was stated straight away that everyone would be given a job offer within the State Security Service of Serbia and that everyone would receive an offer to go on doing the work they had been do doing until then. And that's exactly what was done. As far as I know, and I know definitely what was happening in my department, not a single person was dismissed, removed, whatever you wish to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your department was integrated with which part of the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had an organisational unit of their own that dealt with operative equipment. And as the merge took place, these two units of ours also merged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you get a new boss; or your colleagues from the republican service, did they get a new boss when the two services merged?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? Within the former SFRY, the operative equipment of the federal service, due to the nature of the work it dealt with and in general terms everything it did, it was certainly the most highly developed compared to all the other republican services, including the Serbian one. So the people working in the Serbian department simply -- were simply redeployed in our service. I was the head of the department for the application of operative equipment, and I stayed on in that position. So no one within the 7th Department was removed from the positions they had held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the head of the department for operative equipment from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the people from the republic did not come to work with us. Some of them were transferred to work on teaching jobs in the institute, and their head was appointed advisor. So he did not really join our service, our part of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujovic. You have just mentioned offensive and defensive measures, i.e., the application of offensive as opposed to defensive measures. Can you just briefly tell us what measures would be offensive measures?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In our division, and I believe it is a generally used division for this part of the service, offensive measures are those measures that lead to obtaining intelligence, and that implies interception of all sorts of communications. That also includes documentation, photographic documentation, and things like that. So that would be the category of offensive measures of operative equipment and methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And now, what about defensive measures? What would be the defensive measures of operative work?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: It is a range of measures which is within the purview of the State Security Department, and it applies to the protection of facilities and individuals, as prescribed by the law. That's measures against interception, against biological, chemical protection, technical security, electronic security, mechanical security. So those would be defensive measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, you spent your career in the State Security Service. What is the principle of confidentiality in the State Security Service and similar services?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that everywhere in the world such services are organised in a very similar, if not identical, manner and the principle of confidentiality applies everywhere. This is one of the basic principles that is used in every service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does that principle mean in more specific terms? Let me give you an example: One operative, does he have to know about the work and conducts of another operative? How does that principle apply to that level of the service?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, things like that do not happen unless there is specific interest in exchanging information. When I say interest, I mean operative interest. When it comes to operative equipment and methodologies used, the 7th Administration was a very complex administration in terms of its structure, and in view of the obligations it had, and within the administration itself, the principle of confidentiality and protection was strictly adhered to. Within the 7th Administration, nobody who, for example, dealt with biology, chemistry or counter-division and sabotage was able to know what the first department was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Within the service, who is it who defines the need to collect intelligence by using operative equipment?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: There are linings of work, counter-intelligence, intelligence, then there's also a group that was involved in extremism and counter-terrorism and there was also a group that was involved in the protection of facilities and individuals. What I'm saying is that operative lines defined the need to use and apply operative equipment and methodologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the specific situation, how would that look? For example, if an operative learns that he needs to use operative equipment, what does he have to do in order to apply an operative methodology measure?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: The document that allowed us to apply a certain measure was a decision by the president of the Supreme Court. Before that decision was issued, there was a chain of actions that had to take place in various operative administrations, which means an operative would give his proposal, that goes to the chief, that, again, goes to the chief of administration. So there is a whole chain of decision-making, and the last person was chief of department, and that -- those were all proposals which were sent to the president of the constitutional court of Serbia who made the final decision involving a national of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, I would like to clarify -- to ask you two things: Could you please speak more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters; and, secondly, could you specify the court in question. Who had the final say? The president of which court had the final say when it came to the application of operative equipment and measures?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, the president of the Supreme Court, did he have an office within the service; and did he perform his duties in that office?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to Mr. Stanisic's decision, in our building, there was an ex-territorial space, as it were. That was an office to which only the president of the Supreme Court had a key. He had his office, and he had his documents there, and he was the only person who could independently avail himself of that space.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You have just explained what measures were applied when they were applied against citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Republic of Serbia. Was the same procedure applied against foreign nationals?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the interpretation of the president of the Supreme Court, he was not authorised to decide on measures against foreign nationals. When it came to foreign nationals, the decision was signed by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned a procedure that had to be complied with in the matters of applying operative equipment and -- and -- and measures. Were there any exceptions to that general rule? And the rule was that the president of the Supreme Court of Serbia issued decisions applying to Serbian nationals, and the minister of the interior issued decisions applying to foreign nationals. Were there any exceptions to that principle or to that rule?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: A decision of the president of the Supreme Court was always necessary. However, there were such cases which were urgent, and the procedure could not be complied with fully. Then chiefs of state security centres had the right to issue a temporary measure that was valid for seven days, not longer. And that was done in order not to lose something that was of some importance for the service. However, during that period, they were duty-bound to launch the procedure leading to the decision by the president of the Supreme Court. That decision always had to issue -- always had to be issued. However, when the matter was urgent, temporary measures could be instituted, pending that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, operative equipment and measures, when certain intelligence was obtained, what would operatives do with that intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: The result of offensive application of operative equipment was intelligence. The intelligence would be sent from the administration to the body that requested the application of operative equipment and measures. The -- what happens to that intelligence after that is not something that interested the operatives in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to operative equipment and measures, will -- were operatives interested in the contents of the intelligence obtained?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we take an early break, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take an early break. I take it there are good reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There are. And it's one of the usual complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, we were just discussing the procedure that needs to be adhered to when it comes to the application of technical measures. Tell us, to apply technical measures in respect of a national of ours who is abroad, does that also require an approval to be issued by the Supreme Court?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for our nationals, yes. For those who are abroad, a document had to be issued by the president of the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in respect of an individual who is to have measures applied in -- in his respect, should that individual go abroad? Would it be standard practice for these measures to continue to be applied in respect of that individual even if he is now abroad?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does any sort of approval have to be obtained for conducting surveillance over the radio, be it at home or abroad?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to radio communication, and where intelligence needs to be obtained in an area that is outside of the territory of the Republic of Serbia, that, too, would require an approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what lines of work within the service requested the use of technical equipment?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the basic lines: Intelligence, counter-intelligence, terrorism, and protection from terrorism, as well as the unit - and I think it was the sixth unit - which was charged with protection of persons or vital facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to a question that I put to you a moment ago. When it comes to radio surveillance at home or abroad - we're talking about free radio communication - would the president of the Supreme Court require to be informed of it and issue an approval in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was not required.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, based on whose instructions would the measures of operative work be conducted, and I mean within the 7th Department?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the application of technical measures, it fell solely within the purview of the 7th Department; that's to say, the department for operative equipment. And, of course, it would be the operative service itself that would deal with protection of individuals. There is a certain stage in the application of these measures where you have to have the closest of terms between the operative and the operator of these technical measures, because, of course, the operator would require input from the operative who is working on a particular case as to what his wishes are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am now about to show certain documents to the witness that require us to move into private session, so can we please do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session. And the documents not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, we're going back to the conversation about 1991. Tell us, please, the employees of the federal service of the DB, were they sent to the area of conflict in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Groups were established on the basis of ministerial decision and people were being sent to areas where more serious incidents had occurred in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, while you worked in the federal service of the DB, did you ever report to the higher echelons of the State Security Service or the higher echelons of the ministry itself?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I submitted different reports. There were reports that I knew had to reach the minister, that the minister was bound to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In formal terms, a report of yours that was supposed to reach the minister, what was it supposed to contain, as far as the form of the report itself was concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the procedure of sending these reports was as follows: Since the service operates strictly on the principles of subordination, I could not send a report like that directly to the minister, although I knew that the minister was supposed to see this report. The report was sent by the head of my department. I submit my report to the head of the department. He familiarises himself with it. And then he compiles a document, and then my report is submitted, together with that document, to the minister. That is the usual procedure involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about this accompanying document? What is done with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it includes a number in our register and also a number at the minister's office. And it also denotes the nature of the document involved and the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please look at P3017 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, this is a report that was purportedly compiled by Milorad Davidovic on the 8th of August, 1991. I'm not asking you anything about the content of the report. I would kindly ask you to take a look at the first page and the last page of that report, and I would like to ask you the following: On the basis of your own experience in preparing reports that are supposed to end up on the minister's desk ultimately, on the basis of the form of this document, can one conclude that this report was ever sent to the minister? Could the first page be displayed first and then the last page. And then I would kindly ask you to give us your answer. Could you please take a look at the entire first page.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: It is unusual that someone from the lower structures in the service writes a report and says, Personally to the minister. That is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see anything on this page that would indicate that this report had been registered, sent, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No. As we can all see on our screens, there is no trace of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page now, please. The last page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, my question is the same. On the basis of the form of the last page of this report, can one infer whether this report was ever sent to anyone; and, if so, where and when?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. This was not the practice of the federal service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Vujovic, please look at the upper part of this report. There's some numbers here. Can you interpret that for us? I'm not asking you about the number in red. I'm asking you about the numbers further up, 06-05-05. Can you discern what these numbers are?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: It looks like a fax header. Obviously -- obviously it was not typed up when the document itself was typed up. This was obviously faxed, and it looks like the kind of thing that a fax machine generates on its own. That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 2D1218 would be the document that I'd like to have displayed on our screens now. And I would like to have this document admitted as a Defence exhibit. Actually, this is a bar table submission since it is the reply that our Defence team received from the Republic of Serbia in relation to this report that we dealt with now. 3017, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that this document has very low probative value, if any, and I'd like to briefly explain that. The Davidovic report, which is the subject of the letter, was found to be authentic and reliable by Your Honours in your decision of the 1st of September, 2011. The Chamber took into consideration the evidence provided by Mr. Davidovic, the author of the report, as well as the testimony of DST-034 an exhibits P478 and 489. The Simatovic Defence has not elicited from this witness any additional evidence about which copy this would be. This witness is clearly not placed -- does not have the foundation to comment on it or in -- specifically in a way that would address what Your Honours have already decided in your decision. That's at paragraphs 19 to 21. The letter states that BIA does not have a copy of the report in its archive. This fact is not surprising, especially in light of DST-034's evidence that the reason the Serbian MUP took over the federal MUP was -- or, actually, I won't get into that in front of the witness, but there is some testimony on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Further, the letter that was received did not respond to the question as to whether the document was ever created by the federal MUP. The only information provided was that is was not in BS archives. So, nevertheless, if the Chamber feels it is somewhat relevant, we wouldn't oppose it, but we do question whether it has any probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, at this stage what we're interested in to see whether there where any obstacles to administration, and what are you doing, as a matter of fact, is already weighing evidence and then to say since there is more on the other side, this is of little probative value. I think that's a bit premature. But -- have we seen the document? [Overlapping speakers] ... you asked us to -- to admit from the bar table [Overlapping speakers] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I've got it on my screen now. Let me just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may respond, if you believe it is necessary for me to respond, to what my learned friend said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've not made up -- we have not made up our mind on that yet. Let's first have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will, at a later stage, weigh all the evidence in relation to this document, evidence of whatever kind, but considers that this is a -- may well be a part of the puzzle, and, therefore, is admitting it into evidence. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1218 will receive number D872, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D872 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, we're moving on to the period after the federal and republican services were merged. Can you tell us what things were like now, once you moved into the republican service? How was the work distributed between you and the regional centres within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: As the services were merged, the 7th Department became even busier. Namely, we had to be involved in providing guide-lines, supervision, technical assistance, et cetera, in various centres in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So your 7th Administration continues to do what kind of work directly?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the administration continued doing what had been its main work up until then; and that is to say, the diplomatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, you're saying that centres did a considerable amount of work. These centres, do they submit to the 7th Administration the results of their work after they had applied operative technical measures?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To whom are these results submitted, the ones that technicians in centres obtain?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: They send the results of their work to the operative in that same centre who was in charge of that particular work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, what were all the lines of work within the 7th Administration after the merging of the services?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the same lines of work: Counter-intelligence, intelligence, extremism, terrorism, and also the protection of buildings and individuals. That was line 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you joined the RDB at the end of 1992, in the 7th Administration was there a service, a particular division, for radio monitoring or surveillance?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: You call it a very simple name, radio monitoring, but that was not within the 7th Administration anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Radio monitoring would be of relevance to which administration?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of the radio spectrum and all the beneficiaries of such communications, well, that would practically be only within the remit of the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Radio monitoring, can you tell us just in a few words how this measure can be successfully implemented?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what you keep calling radio monitoring is just part of the work involved in a field that is called monitoring the radio spectrum. Radio monitoring is the initial part of the work that has to be carried out by those who want to monitor the radio spectrum. Radio monitoring is certainly a very demanding thing, very difficult. It requires a great deal of professionalism, a great deal of experience, a great deal of patience. Quite simply, in radio monitoring, you are seeking certain channels, certain frequencies, that may be of interest to the service. And the search itself is very, very, very, delicate, as I've already said, and it is also very strenuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Geographically speaking, where is it best to deploy such equipment for radio monitoring?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the radio spectrum is concerned, according to its physical characteristics, it is very diverse, in terms of how the radio waves spread due to the physics involved. Most of the radio spectrum requires the following: To get as close as possible physically, the best geographical point, as you had put it, in order to be able to monitor the radio spectrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please move into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do so, Mr. Petrovic, if I look at the last two minutes: Can you tell us in a few words how radio monitoring can be successfully implemented. The answer doesn't say a thing about that. It is about that it's not as simple and that it's very delicate and very strenuous. So apparently you are happy with an answer which does not in any way reflect what you apparently are seeking, listening to your question. Then the next one: Geographically speaking, what's the best -- what is it best to deploy equipment. And then "... get as close as possible." Well, is that really information which you think the Chamber would need? I mean, if you want to monitor radio, then it does not really come as a surprise that being closer to it rather than far away is better. And, apart from that, again, I really have difficulties in following the relevance. And if it is relevant, then please try to get an answer to your question rather than to wait for one minute and then accept whatever the witness says, whether or not related to your question. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, I just asked you about the deployment of the equipment in view of the geographical characteristics of the terrain. You said that one should get as close as possible. Does the distance play a role in the choice of equipment? Can some of the equipment be used only when you're closer? Can some others be employed at a certain distance? Can you tell us something about this notion of closeness and distance? For which equipment is it important to be close and what kind of monitoring can be done from a distance? With what equipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the members of your service suggested that interesting intelligence might be obtained through radio monitoring? And was that conveyed to the service employees who were interested in the intelligence that could be obtained through radio monitoring?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, before 1993, the 7th Administration was not involved in that. Later on, as the situation evolved, I know that there was an initiative to monitor the whole radio spectrum -- came from an official of the republican MUP. Can I perhaps say his name? His name was Luki, also known as Lula. He was a ham operator. He was passionate about it and his initiative was prompted by the fact that his colleagues drew attention to the fact in there -- to the fact that in their work they could intercept information that was sent from Bosnia and Herzegovina or perhaps Croatia and that they didn't know what to do with that. And they told him, Okay, you're a member of the service. We're in Belgrade. We're able to intercept that information in terms here in Belgrade. Why don't you say something to somebody? So the initiative was his and those were the circumstances under which the situation developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before you joined the RDB, were there people who heard that Lukic's initiative and did they become engaged in their tasks that I erroneously called radio monitoring?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: What happened next is something that I can tell you from what I heard. The operatives from the intelligence administration wanted to see how the whole thing worked. They then realised that they could, indeed, obtain interesting intelligence in that way, and then they decided under the circumstances to engage that group of ham operators to collect intelligence. And when I joined, after the merger with the republican MUP, that group already existed, and we called them amateurs in our jargon. They had already started collecting intelligence, using their equipment in that area, in the area of radio monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any of the individuals who were members of that group that controlled the radio spectrum?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: There were several of them. But later on I had contacts with two of them: Ranko Tadic, who had a degree in electrical engineering - he was an excellent engineer - and Nikola Varda, who was a watch repairman - he was an excellent ham radio operator. And the two of them were leaders of sorts of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we go back into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, the group that you have just described for us, was it deployed anywhere? Was it stationed anywhere to continue monitoring the radio spectrum?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: From my subsequent conversations with them and when we jointly planned our tasks in a subsequent period, at first, I know that they were deployed or stationed in Pajzos. That was a facility called Pajzos.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did you learn what kind of equipment they had initially?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Initially, since we, as the service, had not been involved in the radio spectrum control, at the very beginning, they had their own equipment. The service provided them with an adapted vehicle. However, when they first started working, they worked on their equipment. Later on, professional equipment was purchased. But at first they used their own equipment and our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a vehicle was that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that they had a Land Rover at that time. And that Land Rover was adapted to accommodate both the equipment and the men who operated the equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to note that this was not at all in the 65 ter summary in relation to this witness. It's all unnoticed evidence, though, also, the relevance is questionable at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please bear with me for a moment, please. Please look at our summary. And in that summary, in the second paragraph, in the third and fourth paragraphs, you will see that those paragraphs contain all this information. There is reference to Pajzos, the significance of radio monitoring. There's also a reference to the adapted Land Rover. And it says here that people who were involved had special expertise but they were not permanent members of the service. All that is contained in our summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The summary focuses on the 7th and 2nd Administrations. I see now the comment about others not employed. Perhaps the problem is generally that there is so little detail that it's really -- this, for example, calling them the amateurs, all of this is specific information that could be included -- that would be included in a statement, and in this way we are continually prejudiced by the lack of notice. But I will not, at this stage, object to the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Petrovic may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, you have told us about this adapted Land Rover vehicle. And you told us that those men were stationed at Pajzos. In geographical terms, why was Pajzos significant, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Pajzos, as I have already told -- told you before, had to do with geography. Tactically it was well located because it covered a large part of Eastern Slavonia, and we're particularly interested in Pajzos because we wanted to chase those link communications; because at the beginning of the conflict, the Croats had re-routed their links. So we were trying to find them, and Pajzos was suitable because we believed that we could intercept some of their communications from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please move into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, did you go to Pajzos once you joined the RDB?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. I was in Pajzos.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The technicians and translators from your administration, did they also go to Pajzos?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Pajzos was a very good point for radio monitoring. And one of its advantages was that you could send translators there to work there because there were accommodation facilities there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did any other employ employees -- as far as you know, any other RDB employees were they deployed in Pajzos when you went there?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: From RDB?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, people from the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, was there an intelligence point at Pajzos?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were there with our equipment which means that it was an intelligence point. It goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, how did intelligence operatives and the employees of your administration co-operate at Pajzos?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, similar organisations was in place in every intelligence point and that applied to Pajzos as well. Since it was not in the centre, the intelligence that was collected through radio monitoring was submitted to the intelligence operative who was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet Franko Simatovic at Pajzos?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how many times and why did you meet Simatovic there?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that happened twice, if I'm not mistaken. It was a long time ago. We had working meetings. We wanted to see if we could do anything else at that place, how many people we should have there, and so on and so forth. Nothing special about those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned equipment that was at Pajzos. Was that mobile or stationary equipment?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: At first, that was mobile equipment, and later on, there came a time when we were able to obtain stationary equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In order to install that equipment, did you have to have antennas and were those antennas visible?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Those antennas were visible. You could not work without antennas, and especially the surveillance antennas that were used in the surveillance systems. In terms of their physical characteristics, they have to be bigger than any other transmitter's antennas, and there's no way you could mask them or disguise them or hide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when you went there? Could you be more specific and tell us what years were those?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I went there in 1994 and 1995, 1996. During that period, I was there twice, I believe. I really don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the equipment with -- electronic surveillance and the operators who used them, do they need to be secured; and, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both people and equipment have to be secured. There's no two ways about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why? Why is that important? Why do men and equipment have to be secured?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: For several reasons: The first is physical protection; the second reason is the confidentiality that we already discussed. That's part of the method of work. Things have to be confidential, secure; hence, the physical security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, you're saying that you went to Pajzos in 1994 and 1995. Who was it who provided security for Pajzos in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: It was an anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How were they engaged? Who was that unit engaged to provide security for the facility at Pajzos? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: That was an independent unit which was an integral part of the State Security Department. The request for their engagement could have been issued by the chief of department or the special advisor, whoever. However, it was the minister who could make the final decision on their engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, you mentioned the adapted Land Rover. Were any other vehicles adapted to suit the purpose of radio monitoring that we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: When we were ordered to organise that part of the activity as part of the 7th Administration, then we hired people, we got vehicles, and as time went on, we ended up with a lot of vehicles, different vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As the equipment for radio monitoring developed, did you develop any other facilities with radio monitoring equipment, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Ranko Tadic and his group. Can you tell us why that group continued to be involved in this work even after your people had started working on it?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, there weren't enough people for this job. We started developing this kind of work in 1993 practically. So we had to organise people and resources as the work went along. This is a very special kind of work. You don't have enough trained personnel to do that. So, quite simply, we never, ever had enough people to meet all the needs of the intelligence line of work. So it was only natural that this team went on working.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am checking the time, and I wonder whether this would be the right time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had a relatively short first session. If we would take a break now we would have a last session of one and a half hour. I would prefer to split up, so if you would go on for six or seven minutes, then we have three sessions divided by two breaks of half an hour. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, how was this agreed upon, getting Ranko Tadic's group to work on this job?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was agreed upon with the intelligence people. A decision was reached who was supposed to go. I already told you. We didn't have enough people. So the questions was whether we should withdraw a group from amongst our permanent personnel or whether we should send ham radio operators. So it always had to do with the assessment of our priorities, what was the priority at a given point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, do you know what the legal basis was for involving the ham radio operators headed by Ranko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they had freelance contracts and they were paid on the basis of such contracts, and that is how they did their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just pause for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to inquire whether the issue of technical means will be returned to, or perhaps we could be in public session for this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we return into public session, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can go back into public session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, you mentioned freelance contracts. Can you tell us which administration within the RDB was in charge of contracting such individuals?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: The 8th Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these individuals received per diems when they were sent out into the field for that period of time that they spent in the field?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who paid these per diems; and can you tell us whether the principle involved was any different from the principle applied in the case of other employees who were sent out into the field?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as per diems were concerned, there was no difference, in principle. It was the 8th Administration that paid all the per diems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5458. Could it please not be displayed to the public. And could we have a look at page 28. Could I please have page 20. The document I want is P5458. P4558 [as interpreted], page 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Just -- if it is of assistance, the document that was noted to us was P458. I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I've been saying that all along. And I would like to see page 20. Your Honours, there is no English translation here on page 20 because this is simply a list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, this is a list that was compiled for having per diems paid. I would like to ask you to take a look at the list and tell us whether you recognise any of the names.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Number 17, Nikola Varda; and Ranko Tadic, number 20. That is what I can see straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise any other names?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Possibly. But these two, yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, Mr. Vujovic. You told us that people who dealt with electronic surveillance were involved in Pljesevica and Petrova Gora. Can you tell us when this actually took place?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: 1994, 1995, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm facing a dilemma now. But I believe that following your instructions from the beginning of the hearing, I think it would be a good thing if we moved into closed session because I'm going to refer to a location where certain measures were being applied, and I'm going to refer to individuals who were involved in that. So following your instructions, I believe it would be a good idea if that were to be discussed in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we will do that after the break. I would have one or two additional questions to seek clarification of the witness. Mr. Vujovic, I take you back to -- well, let's say, approximately a half-hour ago when you commented on the report which you said was at least uncommon because it was directly addressed to the minister. It was the report by Mr. Davidovic. Do you have any personal knowledge about the activities of Mr. Davidovic, or is it just that you commented on the document, as you saw, it without having any knowledge about Mr. Davidovic's activities and this specific report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know even know who Mr. Davidovic is. I didn't know then; I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question relates to the document we just looked at, which is, in order to avoid whatever confusion, is P458, we see a list of 27 names. Is it your testimony that all these persons were involved in surveillance of radio communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That is not what I'm saying. My understanding of the question was as follows: Do I recognise any individuals from this list, and who are these people. And I identified Nikola Varda and Ranko Tadic who were in this group of ham radio operators. Possibly there are some other ham operators here. Who these other people are, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, you couldn't tell us anything about the other persons, what their activities were, whether they were involved in radio communications or other matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you insist, for example, number 1, Milorad Budimir. He worked -- he worked on securing communications for anti-sabotage units. So he was a communications man. I could single him out therefore, but not anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any way you can link these persons to an ATD unit of the MUP? ATD standing for anti-terrorist operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who generated this document. If it was generated by the 8th Administration, that is usually the case when documents dealt with per diems, or if this is from some particular location where an ATD was and whether there was radio surveillance involved. It could have been Pajzos or anywhere else. And then perhaps a composite document was sent for the payment of per diems. I don't see any other possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does your answer mean that intercepting or monitoring radio communications was part of the anti-terrorist operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Intercepting communications is handled by the intelligence administration. As I've already said, and as I saw in Pajzos, there was a unit for providing physical security for this intelligence point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you protect the -- this point with staff from the -- or people involved in the anti-terrorist operations unit? Is that logical, to give them a task in securing such a facility as you'd described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand what you said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me check your last answer then. I asked you whether "monitoring radio communication was part of the anti-terrorist operations." You said: "Intercepting communications is handled by the intelligence administration." And then you said: As I told you already, in Pajzos, there was a unit for providing physical security for this intelligence point. Now I earlier -- understood your earlier answers that the intelligence point was primarily monitoring radio communications because that was such an excellent place. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood that well, Your Honour, and that is exactly what I had said. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my question was -- you introduced, then, the physical security of those involved in this monitoring of communications. And my question was: Would you use an anti-terrorist operations units to secure a facility in which monitoring radio communications is the main thing to be done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my answer would be affirmative. The unit at Pajzos was in charge of providing physical security for the facility. External physical security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were these members of the anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to that. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. May we kindly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did the intelligence from Pljesevica go to?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: The intelligence from Pljesevica went to the operative on Petrova Gora, along the operative work line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we confer, and if we do not ask you to stop, then we will re-read the transcript, the five lines we are missing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujovic, according to what you know, was there an intelligence point on Mount Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? How do you know things about Pljesevica and Petrova Gora? Do you have first-hand knowledge, or did you learn it from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: I have first-hand knowledge about Petrova Gora because I was involved in the planning and sending men who worked there for a fortnight or longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at -- or, rather, before that, I have another question for you in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the third division of the 7th Administration. When was it set up, the third division, and how did it develop over time?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already told you, the 7th Administration was not involved in radio monitoring and radio spectrum surveillance until the moment that the two services were merged in Serbia. And then an initiative was launched --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm just interested in the time-period.

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: That's was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After the third division was set up, in view of the nature of their work, could ham radio operators be members of the team of the 7th Administration?

utterances.speaker: RADE VUJOVIC
utterances.text: In -- in a functional sense, they were members of the team, but they were not on permanent contracts. When it came to planning and sending people into the field, we always had made arrangements with the intelligence as to where people would go because we did not have enough men. But, in formal terms, they were never permanent members of the 7th Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I just wanted some clarification. I looked in the transcript - maybe I missed it - but I can't find the witness having mentioned the third division. So it's leading, but also just unclear, exactly, if that is referring to these amateurs that he was talking about, or what it's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, I would like to add to, what Ms. Friedman just said, one comment. We are interested primarily in facts. For example, if the witness says, I have first-hand knowledge about Petrova Gora because I was involved in the planning in sending men who worked there for a fortnight or longer, what I'm interested to know is how many men did he send there? What was the average number of people working there? Were they technicians? Were they translators? Because it seems that, if I understand you well, it's -- the Defence is eliciting evidence which shows the presence and the activities of radio monitoring people in that places you refer to. Now, whether there were or not may be relevant. Perhaps even more relevant is whether they were exclusively there or whether there were others, and what the others were doing as well. Now by hearing about I didn't have enough people. Enough. What is enough? Give me the numbers. Give me also for those who were sent there. If the witness could tell us how many people he sent to Petrova Gora, then I would be happy because that gives me at least some of the information I would need. So, therefore, I -- when you said you were involved in the planning and sending of people to Petrova Gora, how many -- I think you called them ham monitoring or -- these technician who do the technical work in monitoring the -- the radio range, how many people did you send to Petrova Gora? How many would be there, on average? Two, five, ten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You put it well, Your Honour. The average number changed from one situation to the next. However, if we are talking about averages, I would say that a minimum number would be four or five men who were on Petrova Gora mount at any one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know how many support, in terms of translators, were sent to Petrova Gora, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were one or two translators, not more. We did not have any -- any more of them on our team, or available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then understand well that, on average, for performing the radio communication monitoring would take some seven people on average, the presence of seven people, on average, in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that -- you can put it that way, at least for this particular part of the whole exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us detailed information as how many people were there to secure the equipment and the -- and the persons performing that job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you. I personally never went to Petrova Gora, so I wouldn't be able to share that information with you. Even if I'd gone there, chances are I would have never been aware of that particular figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
